The wish that opens the chapter separates the commentators into two camps that never meet. Gill reads it as the church asking Christ to stand toward her as a brother, notes that several Jewish writers grant the King Messiah is meant, and reports that many of the ancients took the verse for the old church's longing for the incarnation. Henry works the same allegory harder and more precisely: the spouse is betrothed but not yet married, the nuptials being reserved for the second coming, and so must keep a certain distance — which is why she wishes for the innocent freedom a sister has with a brother who fed at the same breast. He allows the older reading, that this is the prayer of the Old Testament saints for a hastened incarnation, but prefers to make it every believer's wish for closer communion. Wesley compresses the whole to a desire for stricter union.

Against them stand three who read a woman and a man. Clarke has the bride afraid that her fondness will look like excessive familiarity, and wishing her lover were a small brother so that she might kiss him in the street without offending anyone. Ellicott makes the verse a recollection: the poet has her remember what she felt before the obstacles to their union were cleared, when she could not avow her love openly and wished their relation had allowed an embrace without reproach — and he notes the marginal rendering, that they, meaning her family, would not then have reproached her. Delitzsch begins by stating the plain fact the allegory has to work around, that Solomon is not her brother, and explains the wish as a dream carrying her into the reality she wanted, so that she has in him what a brother is to a sister; the Hebrew particle, he adds, means not as though but in the manner of.

The mother's house divides them the same way. Gill takes the mother for the church of the firstborn, in which believers are born and brought up, and reads the leading as prayer, since great persons are led; Wesley offers an alternative rendering in which the house is where she was educated, and makes the drink stand for gifts and graces employed in Christ's service. Clarke and Ellicott keep to the household. Clarke explains that the mother would teach her how to behave toward her husband as she once taught her to nurse a child, and identifies the spiced wine as a strong invigorating drink shared from one cup by bride and bridegroom on the wedding day, a sign that they were to bear the comforts and adversities of life together. Ellicott quotes a traveller on eastern beverages, who found sherbet of pomegranate juice the best of them for its cooling acidity.

Two structural observations close the group. Clarke, who reads the book as a wedding-week drama, marks the end of the sixth night at the fourth verse. Delitzsch marks a different seam, noting that the sixth act opens with the same question that opened the third, and that where the earlier one closed the account of a love still growing, this one closes the account of a love consummated. He adds a text-critical curiosity: the Greek translator, faced with illegible consonants, produced clothed in white where the Hebrew has coming up out of the wilderness. On the smaller matter of the embrace Gill notes that the clause may be a petition, that his hand would be under her head, or a statement that it already is; Ellicott simply refers the charge to the daughters of Jerusalem back to its earlier occurrences.
5:
Who asks the question about the woman coming up from the wilderness is disputed. Gill, Clarke and Henry give it to the daughters of Jerusalem, who have just been charged and now look at her with admiration; Henry mentions the alternative, that the bridegroom is expressing pleasure at her reliance, and rejects it, adding that angels and friends are alike joyful spectators. Wesley takes the view Henry rejects, noting that a Hebrew speaker may refer to himself in the third person. On the wilderness the schools part again: for Gill and Henry it is the world and the state of sin, barren and without true comfort, out of which a soul is carried in Christ's arms; for Clarke it is the country, from which the bride returns on her lover's arm.

The apple tree is obscure in the Hebrew, and everyone says so. Clarke offers a nearly literal rendering in which the man excited her to espouse him there and her mother contracted her on the same spot, then an alternative in which he found her asleep under the tree and woke her, the place happening to be where her mother bore her; the Latin, he notes, gives the clause an abominable meaning. Ellicott takes the verb as arousing a passion, and records that the Greek adds shining white. Wesley allegorises: the raising is from death in trespasses, the shadow is Christ's own, and the tree under which the mother bore her is the church. It is here that Ellicott states his method. This section, he says, opens the most magnificent description of true love ever written; the dramatic theory meets insuperable difficulties with it, and the theatre and spectators must be imaginary — the poet recalls leading his bride through the scenes of their shared youth before breaking into praise of the passion that joined them.

The seal draws four pictures. Delitzsch keeps to the object, a signet-ring worn on a cord at the breast or on the hand, and reads the request as her answer to a recollection of how their love began. Gill looks to the high priest, who carried the tribes' names on stones over heart and shoulders, and mentions lovers who wore names or portraits on the arm — not, he insists, signets. Clarke reports what he has seen in the Levant, where figures are pricked into the skin and rubbed with a blue powder that lodges beneath and stays distinct for life, and thinks the bride asks to be marked so on the arm always before her lover's eyes and on the breast that stands for her share in his heart. Wesley takes it for an engraved tablet and a signet on the hand.

On the great lines about love the commentary is lexical, and Ellicott has most to say. The word rendered jealousy, he argues, means ardent passion rather than suspicion, as the parallel shows — strong as death is love, inexorable as the grave is ardent passion — and he traces it to a root meaning to be red with flame. The coals are named by a word used elsewhere of thunderbolts, sparks and the burning heat of fever; and the closing phrase, which the English makes a most vehement flame, is literally a flame of Jah, the only divine name in the book, used to express something superlatively strong. He also corrects the seventh verse's last clause, where the Hebrew doubles the verb, so the man himself would be utterly despised. Clarke turns that into advice: pure love cannot be bought, whatever old rich men hope from loading young women with presents, since affection cannot be commanded even by one who feels it. Gill and Wesley read the waters and floods as persecution and temptation, and Gill adds what gives the allegory its force: a believer's love may be left but not lost, its fervency abated while the thing remains.
8:
Ellicott opens the section by admitting a problem. Commentators are almost unanimous, he says, that the poem properly ends at the seventh verse; those who construct it as a drama find no place for what follows except as a meaningless epilogue, its want of cohesion is so plain that many reject it as a later addition, and others rescue it by rearranging the whole book. His own account removes the difficulty by removing the plot: if the sections are successive presentations of one story of courtship and marriage, set down as they occurred to the poet, nothing here is out of place. Clarke, reading the book as a wedding drama, takes the sister at face value, a girl of the bride's household not yet marriageable whose hand will one day be asked for. Gill and Henry make her the Gentile church as the Jewish church sees her — little, on Henry's account, because undignified by the knowledge of God, without breasts because without revelation, scriptures or ministry — and Henry frames the passage as a couple consulting about their affairs, yoke-fellows who having laid their hearts together now lay their heads together.

The wall and the door are read as alternatives, and the question is what they measure. Ellicott makes them chastity and its opposite: if the girl grows up inaccessible to seduction her brothers will build on her so an illustrious house may spring from her, and if not they will take the strongest precautions to guard her honour — a passage he calls one of the best arguments for reading the book as a celebration of chaste wedded love. He mentions and dismisses an attempt to explain the silver palace from a Druse ornament worn like a horn. Delitzsch supplies the social fact, that brothers are a sister's nearest guardians and in marriage precede even father and mother, and defends the construction as a genuine contrast against a scholar who denied it can express one. Clarke reports Calmet's version, in which an unmarried woman is a wall without towers, a door without a bar, a city without defences, so the brothers must find a rich and powerful husband.

Her reply is taken three ways. Ellicott has the heroine break in with a protest of her purity and her right to marry, being of age and knowing herself beloved. Clarke reads an argument from her own case — she became marriageable, needed the protection she now enjoys, and was given in marriage as soon as she pleased her lover — offered so the same may be arranged for her sister. Delitzsch turns it toward the brothers, since she compares herself with the younger girl and refers the credit she claims to their care. Gill and Wesley allegorise: for Wesley these are the Jewish church's words, that by grace she is already what she would have her sister become, while Gill offers the alternative that she wishes rather than asserts.

The vineyard divides them most sharply. Ellicott makes it a repudiation: let Solomon keep his possessions, his harem of mercenary beauties, which cost so much to obtain and keep, since the speaker is happier in the secure love of one true wife — and he reads the two hundred paid the keepers as designed to show what a polygamous establishment on that scale costs. Clarke reaches nearly the same place through Calmet, who has the speaker decline both vineyard and profits, satisfied with his own and unwilling to exchange his beloved for all the riches of the universe. Delitzsch reads a request instead, Shulamith turning to her royal husband with her brothers in mind. Gill and Wesley take Solomon for a type of Christ and the vineyard for the church, Wesley adding the point on which the allegory turns, that Christ's title is better because his vineyard was bought not with money but with blood.
13:
Who speaks the thirteenth verse is not settled even in the Greek. Gill points out that the Hebrew participle is feminine and so must address the woman, but records that the Septuagint made it masculine and that Ambrose accordingly read it as the church speaking to Christ, while two other ancient translators took it the other way. Wesley and Henry agree with Gill that Christ is the speaker, and Henry builds the parting scene out of it: the spouse must stay below in the gardens of the earth where she has work to do, while he removes to the mountains of spices to act as her advocate, and he asks to hear from her often — she is ready at her pen, she knows how to direct her letters, and Christ's friends ought to keep a good correspondence with one another as well as with him. Wesley makes the plural of gardens stand for the many congregations, and reads the request for her voice as a request for prayer, praise and the preaching of the gospel while he is away.

The other reading keeps it in the house. Clarke takes the verse for the bridegroom asking his wife's leave to withdraw early in the morning, as was his custom, with the companions waiting to hear and himself hoping the word will be permission to go. Ellicott moves it further back still, making it one more reminiscence of courtship, when the lover envied everyone who stood near the girl, the companions who could see and hear her, and longed for the tokens of affection she was spending on them.

The last verse is a dismissal or an invitation depending on who is being sent away. Delitzsch reports one scholar's view that she is bidding him leave her, though not harshly, since she still calls him her beloved, and another's that the exchange is bantering coquetry; he then makes the objection that decides it for him, that if the request came from Solomon — and he refuses the imaginary shepherd some readers introduce into this closing scene against the plain words about a thousand being Solomon's — then to ignore it would be scornful, since singing unasked to please her friends would be unseemly and silence under her husband's request would be wilful. Clarke reads it simply as permission granted with a plea for a quick return, admits that nobody can identify the mountains of spices beyond supposing them named for the trees that grew there, and marks the end of the seventh night of the marriage week. Ellicott hears in it the answer at last given to the lover's sighing, notes that the received English is better here than the margin, and closes by saying that the poem ends with two short verses compressing everything the book has told repeatedly under other figures, the wooing and the wedding of two happy souls.

The allegorists finish elsewhere. Gill refers the haste either to the incarnation, or to Christ's presence among his people, or to the first spread of the gospel. Wesley makes it a prayer that the work in the world be finished quickly so that the church may be taken to himself. Against all of them stands Clarke's closing note, which is the plainest statement of method anywhere in these commentaries. He calls the book the oldest pastoral in the world and, whatever species of writing it belongs to, beyond controversy the finest and most sublime for imagery and colouring that ever came from a human pen — and then states that throughout his notes he has carefully avoided every attempt to spiritualize it.
